Amsterdam at the centre is the chart's name for the long period, about 1585 to 1780, when Amsterdam and the Dutch Republic led the world economy. For Fernand Braudel it was the last time a single city ran the whole system.

The start is the fall of Antwerp to Spanish troops in 1585, after which merchants, money and skilled workers moved north to Amsterdam, a city of the rebel provinces fighting Spain. The Dutch already had the "mother trade": carrying Baltic grain and timber to western and southern Europe in cheap, efficient ships.

What they built on it:

  • The Dutch East India Company (VOC), founded in 1602, took over much of the Asian spice trade from Portugal, by trade and by force.
  • The Bank of Amsterdam (1609) gave merchants a sound money of account.
  • The Amsterdam Exchange traded goods, bills and company shares every day.
  • Warehouses that stored the goods of the world, so prices across Europe were set there. The tulip mania of 1637 shows how far speculation could go.

The 1600s were the Dutch Golden Age, of Rembrandt, Vermeer and a free press. After about 1670 the Dutch faced English and French power and high costs at home. Amsterdam turned more and more to lending, including to Britain. The end date marks the Fourth Anglo-Dutch War of 1780 to 1784, which ruined Dutch shipping, and the centre passed to London.
sum: Amsterdam at the centre is the chart's name for the long period, about 1585 to 1780, when Amsterdam and the Dutch Republic led the world economy. For Fernand Braudel it was the last time a single city ran the whole system.
